items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I was allowed to stay with the Wade family which consisted of Mr. Wade, his mother and his son.

ctx.x: The Huston's were from way down South and their son came to Cincinnati to live with them after we had been living on Hathaway Street a few months. This fellow was older than I and he loved to carry a pistol. He and I worked at this fruit sugar-coating factory which was at least 6 miles from where we lived. We rode the street car to work and walked home when the work day was finished. My sister stayed with us sometimes and with my mother at times.

My father was offered a job by a rich family near Lexington, Ky., as a cook and he accepted. He rented our apartment to a man named Wade and took my brother to Kentucky with him. My sister went back to stay with my mother and I was allowed to stay with the Wade family which consisted of Mr. Wade, his mother and his son. My father allowed me to stay because I was working, but he told me that if anything went wrong, I should come back to Kentucky.

After Mr. Wade was in our place a certain time, he started making bootleg whiskey. There were barrels of mash in the small room where the man had lived before he moved. He had a copper still that fitted on the gas stove. Mr. Wade started doing good business and I remember that a prohibition officer used to come there at times and drink with Mr. Wade. I used to taste the alcohol when it was hot and dripping from the still.
